lesson.title: Collision Theory: Why Bumping Into Each Other Isn't Enough
lesson.summary: Explains reaction rate at the particle level, showing that reactions require collisions, but also that the overwhelming majority of collisions fail to produce any product at all.
lesson.body:
Everything covered so far in this unit, integrated rate laws, half-life, graphical analysis, describes the mathematics of how concentration changes over time. None of it explains why a reaction proceeds at a particular rate in the first place, at the level of individual particles bumping into one another. That physical picture is called collision theory, and it builds directly on kinetic molecular theory, which already establishes that particles in a gas or in solution are in constant, random motion, colliding with one another extremely frequently, and that not all particles move at the same speed. Instead, particles in any sample exist across a whole distribution of speeds and kinetic energies at a given temperature.

Collision theory's central claim is straightforward: a chemical reaction can only happen when reactant particles physically collide with one another. This immediately explains something you have likely taken for granted in the rate laws studied so far, namely why increasing concentration increases rate. More particles crammed into the same volume simply collide with each other more often, which gives more opportunities for reaction.

But collision theory also explains a genuine puzzle that concentration alone cannot account for: measured reaction rates are almost always dramatically slower than the total collision frequency would predict if every single collision produced product. Something is filtering out the overwhelming majority of collisions before they ever have a chance to react. Two separate conditions must both be satisfied for a collision to be effective, meaning capable of producing product: the colliding particles need to bring enough kinetic energy to the collision, and they need to strike each other in a favorable relative orientation. Fail either requirement, and the particles simply bounce apart chemically unchanged, exactly like billiard balls colliding on a table.

To see just how selective this filtering really is, consider a typical gas phase reaction, using illustrative, order of magnitude numbers rather than data tied to any specific named reaction. Collision theory predicts a staggering total collision frequency, on the order of 1.0 x 10^30 collisions occurring per liter every second, simply from how crowded and fast moving gas molecules are at ordinary pressure. Yet the measured rate of product formation for a typical modest reaction might correspond to only about 1.0 x 10^19 successful, product forming collisions per liter each second. Dividing the two gives the effective fraction:

1.0 x 10^19 / 1.0 x 10^30 = 1.0 x 10^-11

In other words, only about one collision in one hundred billion actually produces a new molecule. That enormous gap between the total collision frequency and the effective collision rate is exactly what the energy requirement and the orientation requirement, taken up formally in the next several sections, exist to explain. The next section names and quantifies the energy half of that requirement, activation energy, and the final section of this unit returns to combine both requirements together with numbers that trace directly back to this same 1.0 x 10^-11 figure.
